title: Add Digits
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated digit folding versus the digital root formula.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a non-negative number, repeatedly add its digits together until only a single digit remains, then return that digit.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Digital root: a repeated digit-summing simulation that is fully replaceable by a closed form modulo 9 identity."],["Difficulty","Beginner"],["Tags","Math"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing the digital root and modulo 9 connection, and correctly handling the num = 0 and multiple-of-9 special cases in the formula."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a non-negative number num, repeatedly add all of its digits together until only a single digit remains, then return that digit.

blocks.title: Analogy: Melting Coins Into a Smaller Stack
blocks.text: Picture melting down a handful of coins and recasting them into a single new coin worth the sum of the old ones, then repeating that process on whatever new coin comes out. Melt a stack representing 38 (recast from a 3 coin and an 8 coin) into an 11 coin, then melt that 11 coin (from a 1 and a 1) into a 2 coin. Once only one coin is left, that is the final answer, there is nothing more to melt down.

blocks.caption: Keep summing digits until only one digit is left

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: num = 38

blocks.content: {"headers":["Round","Number","Digit sum","Why"],"rows":[["1","38","3 + 8 = 11","38 has two digits, so one folding round is applied."],["2","11","1 + 1 = 2","11 still has two digits, so a second round is needed to reach a single digit."]]}

blocks.text: 11 still has more than one digit, so a second round is needed. The final single digit result is 2.
Example: num = 132

blocks.content: {"headers":["Round","Number","Digit sum","Why"],"rows":[["1","132","1 + 3 + 2 = 6","A single round already produces one digit, so folding stops immediately."]]}

blocks.text: A single round already produces a single digit, 6, so no further rounds are needed.
Example: num = 0
Zero is already a single digit, so the answer is simply 0 with no summing needed at all.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what repeated digit folding is actually preserving.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Repeatedly summing digits and replacing the number with that sum always eventually produces a single digit, since the digit sum of a number is always smaller than the number itself once it has two or more digits.

Observation 2: Every place value in a base 10 number, ones, tens, hundreds, and so on, leaves a remainder of exactly 1 when divided by 9, since 10 itself leaves a remainder of 1.

Observation 3: That means a number and the sum of its digits always leave the exact same remainder when divided by 9, no matter how the digits are grouped or how many folding rounds happen.

Observation 4: Since folding never changes the remainder modulo 9, the final single digit answer is fully determined by that one remainder, no actual folding needs to happen.
That reasoning alone already points straight at a formula: read the remainder modulo 9 directly, skip the folding entirely.
6. Brute Force Solution
The most direct approach is to repeat the folding process described in the problem exactly as stated: sum the digits, replace the number with that sum, and repeat until only one digit remains.
Step by step algorithm

items: While num has 10 or more (meaning more than one digit), sum its individual digits.
Extract each digit with num mod 10, then remove it with num divided by 10.
Replace num with that digit sum.
Repeat until num is a single digit, then return it.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: fold the number down one round at a time

codes.python:
def add_digits(num):
    while num >= 10:              # keep folding as long as more than one digit remains
        digit_sum = 0
        temp = num
        while temp > 0:
            digit_sum += temp % 10  # peel off the last digit and add it in
            temp //= 10               # drop that digit and look at what's left
        num = digit_sum              # replace num with the sum of its digits
    return num                      # single digit remains


if __name__ == "__main__":
    num = 38
    print(add_digits(num))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The outer loop condition checks num >= 10, chosen to read directly as "still has more than one digit."
A separate inner loop and digit_sum variable compute one full folding round before ever reassigning num, so digits are never summed against a partially updated number.
temp is used as a throwaway copy for digit extraction so the outer loop's own num is never touched until the entire digit sum for that round is known.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because it is a literal, repeated application of the rule given in the problem, and every round strictly shrinks the number until a single digit is reached.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log num). Digit summing shrinks a number so aggressively (a d-digit number sums to at most 9d) that only a handful of rounds are ever needed, and each round costs O(log num) to walk the digits.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: this result, called the digital root of a number, follows an exact, well known mathematical pattern related to remainders when dividing by 9, meaning it can be computed directly with a single formula instead of simulating any folding at all.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why folding repeatedly works but is not necessary: every round only ever computes the same remainder modulo 9 that the original number already had.

What the folding is really preserving: the number's remainder when divided by 9, unchanged across every round, all the way down to the final single digit.

Can that remainder be read directly, without folding: yes, since every place value contributes a remainder of exactly 1 modulo 9, a number's own remainder modulo 9 already equals its digital root's remainder.

What about the special case where the remainder is 0: a positive number can never have a digital root of 0, so a 0 remainder actually means the true digital root is 9, not 0.

The core idea: compute 1 plus (num minus 1) mod 9 directly, handling num = 0 as its own base case.

Since 10 leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 9, every place value in a base 10 number (ones, tens, hundreds, ...) is also congruent to 1 modulo 9. That means a number and the sum of its digits always leave the same remainder when divided by 9, no matter how many folding rounds it takes to reach a single digit.

The optimization is to skip the folding entirely and compute that remainder directly, adjusting only for the special case where the remainder would come out as 0 for a positive number (which should map to 9, not 0, since a positive number always has a positive digital root).
9. Optimized Solution
If num is 0, the answer is 0 directly. Otherwise, the answer is 1 plus (num minus 1) modulo 9, a formula known as the digital root formula.
Dry run for num = 38

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Computation","Value","Why"],"rows":[["1","num minus 1","37","Shifting down by 1 before the modulo is what remaps a would-be 0 remainder into 9 instead."],["2","37 mod 9","1","The remainder after the shift."],["3","1 plus 1","2","Shifting back up by 1 restores the correct digital root."]]}

blocks.text: The formula gives 2 directly, matching the two-round folding result from the earlier dry run.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one formula replaces every folding round

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because every power of 10 is congruent to 1 modulo 9 (10 mod 9 = 1, 100 mod 9 = 1, and so on), so a number's value modulo 9 is always identical to the sum of its digits modulo 9, and therefore identical to what repeated digit folding eventually converges to. The only adjustment needed is for numbers that are themselves exact multiples of 9, where the raw remainder would be 0, but a positive multiple of 9 always folds down to 9 itself, never 0, which is exactly why the formula shifts by subtracting 1 before the modulo and adding 1 back after.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["num is 0","Handled as its own explicit base case","0"],["num is a positive multiple of 9","(num minus 1) mod 9 gives 8, plus 1 gives exactly 9","9, never 0"],["num is any other positive number","(num minus 1) mod 9 gives one less than num's true remainder modulo 9, plus 1 restores it","num's digital root directly"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The num == 0 check is a dedicated early return, since the general formula (num minus 1) mod 9 would otherwise try to compute a negative number's modulo, which behaves inconsistently across languages.
Subtracting 1 before taking the modulo, then adding 1 back after, is specifically what remaps a raw remainder of 0 into 9 instead, since a positive number's digital root is never actually 0.
The entire computation is two arithmetic operations, no loop, no digit extraction of any kind.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), a single subtraction and a single modulo operation, regardless of how large num is.
Space: O(1). This is already the theoretical floor, there is no further optimization possible beyond a constant number of arithmetic operations.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is recognizing that a repeated, simulated process (folding digits) can sometimes be replaced by a closed form mathematical identity, in this case tied to remainders modulo 9. Spotting that connection is what turns an O(log num) simulation into an O(1) formula.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the num = 0 special case, which the general formula does not handle correctly on its own.
Writing 1 plus num mod 9 instead of 1 plus (num minus 1) mod 9, which gives the wrong answer whenever num is itself already a multiple of 9.
Assuming the brute force loop is wrong just because it is slower, it is fully correct, just not the most efficient approach.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is often used specifically to see whether a candidate recognizes the digital root pattern, since the brute force loop is trivial to write. Mentioning the connection to modulo 9 and explaining why it works, rather than just producing the formula from memory, demonstrates real mathematical insight.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid looping entirely", think: the digital root formula, 1 plus (num minus 1) mod 9.
If the interviewer says "why does this relate to 9", think: every power of 10 leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 9.
If the interviewer says "what about multiples of 9", think: their digital root is 9, never 0, which is exactly what the formula's shift by 1 is designed to fix.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you explain why every number's digital root only depends on its remainder modulo 9?
What is the digital root of a number in a base other than 10, say base 16?
Can you compute the digital root of a number given only as a string, too large to fit in a normal integer type?
Why does the formula subtract 1 before taking the modulo and add 1 back afterward, instead of just using num mod 9 directly?
How would you verify the digital root formula is correct for every number from 1 to 100 without folding each one by hand?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any problem where a repeated simulation converges to something already determined by a simpler, fixed property of the input, checking for that property directly instead of simulating.
Modular arithmetic tricks in general, remainders modulo a fixed base reappearing across checksum, hashing, and divisibility problems.
Fixed point and convergence problems, where repeating an operation on a number eventually stabilizes, and the interesting question becomes what value it stabilizes to, not how many rounds it takes.
The same off-by-one remainder shift used here, subtract 1, mod, add 1 back, reappears in any 1-indexed modular cycle, such as mapping values into a fixed size range that starts at 1 instead of 0.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force folding approach runs in O(log num) time and O(1) space. The digital root formula runs in O(1) time and O(1) space, a genuine complexity class improvement achieved by recognizing the underlying modulo 9 pattern instead of simulating the process.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: digital root, a repeated digit-summing simulation that always converges to a value fully determined by the number's remainder modulo 9.

Core Idea: since every power of 10 is congruent to 1 modulo 9, a number and the sum of its digits always share the same remainder modulo 9, so the final single digit answer can be read directly from that remainder without ever folding.
Time: O(log num) for the brute force, O(1) for the formula.
Space: O(1) for both.
Most Important Observation: repeated folding never changes the number's remainder modulo 9, it only shrinks the number, so the remainder alone already determines the final answer.

Interview Difficulty: easy to simulate correctly, but recognizing the modulo 9 connection, and the off-by-one adjustment for multiples of 9, is what separates a memorized formula from real understanding.
One line memory trick: digital root equals 1 plus (num minus 1) mod 9, and 0 stays 0.
